nameStory: The name 'cinquefoil' comes from the French 'cinq feuilles,' meaning 'five leaves,' referring to the plant's distinctive five-leaflet pattern. 'Dwarf' distinguishes this shorter species from its taller cousin, common cinquefoil. The scientific name 'canadensis' honors its North American origins, though it's found well beyond Canada's borders.
description: Dwarf cinquefoil is a low-growing perennial wildflower that hugs the ground with trailing stems and cheerful yellow flowers. This member of the rose family spreads by runners, forming loose mats rarely more than 6 inches tall. Each bright yellow flower has five heart-shaped petals that bloom from spring through early summer. The distinctive leaves are divided into five leaflets arranged like fingers on a hand, giving the plant its 'five-leaf' name.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Five leaflets arranged like fingers on a hand, each leaflet oval with toothed edges and a soft, slightly fuzzy texture when you run your finger along the surface

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers with five rounded, slightly notched petals about half an inch across, blooming singly on slender stems above the foliage

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, creeping plant that spreads by runners along the ground, rarely reaching more than 6 inches tall but spreading outward to form loose patches

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Slender, trailing reddish stems that root at joints where they touch the soil, feeling slightly rough to the touch with fine hairs

habitat: Dwarf cinquefoil thrives in poor, dry soils where other plants struggle, making it common along roadsides, in old fields, and sandy areas. You'll often find it in disturbed sites, trail edges, and open woodlands throughout New England. It's actually an indicator of impoverished soil conditions, popping up in places where the earth has been compacted or nutrients depleted.

seasonality.spring: Bright yellow flowers begin appearing in late spring, with the five-fingered leaves emerging fresh and green from overwintering roots.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming continues into early summer, with flowers producing small dry fruits. The plant spreads actively by runners during this season.
seasonality.fall: Foliage may turn reddish or bronze before dying back, though some leaves may persist in protected areas through mild weather.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to the root system, leaving only dried stems and occasional persistent leaves as evidence of the spreading patches underneath.

funFact: This humble little plant serves as the exclusive host for a tiny wasp that creates peculiar round galls on its buds - the cinquefoil bud gall wasp literally redesigns the plant's growth to create a perfect nursery for its babies, turning what would be a flower bud into a protective green marble.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with common cinquefoil, but dwarf cinquefoil stays much lower to the ground and has more trailing, rooting stems. Remember: dwarf hugs the dirt, while common cinquefoil stands more upright. Wild strawberry also has similar leaves, but strawberry has three leaflets instead of five, and white flowers instead of yellow.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being in the rose family, cinquefoils look nothing like garden roses - they're more closely related to strawberries and share that family's characteristic five-petaled flowers. Native American groups like the Iroquois traditionally used the roots medicinally, recognizing properties in this common plant that modern botany has yet to fully explore.
compareHints: Among New England's cinquefoils, dwarf cinquefoil is distinguished by its truly prostrate, mat-forming habit with rooting runners. Common cinquefoil grows more upright, while sulphur cinquefoil is much taller with pale yellow flowers. The silvery cinquefoil has distinctive white-fuzzy leaf undersides that dwarf cinquefoil lacks.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Sulphur cinquefoil stands out from other New England cinquefoils primarily by its bright yellow flowers and consistently five-fingered leaves.

Among New England's cinquefoils, silvery cinquefoil is the only one with dramatically silver-white fuzzy leaf undersides - dwarf and common cinquefoil have plain green undersides, while rough cinquefoil has much larger, coarsely-toothed leaves.
Common cinquefoil differs from dwarf cinquefoil by its longer, more obvious runners and slightly larger flowers.
Unlike other cinquefoils in its genus which typically have five-part leaves (the name cinquefoil means 'five leaves'), mock strawberry has three-part leaves like true strawberries.
Unlike most other New England cinquefoils which have five leaflets, rough cinquefoil stands out with just three leaflets per leaf.
Lesser mock-strawberry differs from other cinquefoils by having three-part leaves instead of the typical five-part leaves (cinque means five in French).
Unlike its lowland cinquefoil relatives that spread by runners or grow as larger plants, dwarf mountain cinquefoil forms tiny, tight cushions and never leaves the alpine zone.

Among New England's cinquefoils, creeping cinquefoil is unique for its long trailing runners and five-leaflet leaves – most other cinquefoils like common cinquefoil and dwarf cinquefoil have three leaflets and don't spread by runners.

Intermediate cinquefoil differs from common New England cinquefoils like dwarf cinquefoil by its specific leaflet count and arrangement, and from sulphur cinquefoil by its smaller stature and different leaf texture.
Unlike its inland cinquefoil relatives, coast cinquefoil has adapted specifically to maritime conditions with its more compact, mat-forming growth and thicker, more succulent-like leaves.
